# UN Climate Talks Start in a Year of Disasters, Energy Price Shocks and Heat Waves
By The Associated Press

(Fetch tool returned a condensed rendering; text below is as returned.)

The 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) begins Monday in Antalya, Turkey, amid accelerating global warming and multiple crises affecting energy systems worldwide.

The world has surpassed the 1.5-degree Celsius warming threshold established in 2015. Currently at 1.4°C of warming, projections indicate the planet is heading toward 2.6°C by century's end. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to be the second year exceeding the 1.5-degree level.

Visible impacts include "Europe's deadly summer heat waves and Nepal's devastating flooding."

Harjeet Singh, founding director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, emphasizes that "Unless and until we resolve the issue of fossil fuel phase out, we will not be able to deal with the problem."

The U.N. estimates global fossil fuel subsidies reached $1.1 trillion this year.

Rather than replacing fossil fuels entirely, nations are using both renewable and conventional energy sources simultaneously to meet growing demand from artificial intelligence and economic development.

The world's largest historical carbon polluter skipped last year's COP and isn't expected to participate this year, complicating funding discussions for climate action in developing nations.

Renewable energy costs have dropped significantly, and electric vehicle adoption continues growing, strengthening economic arguments for transitioning away from fossil fuels.

Turkey is promoting an initiative to increase electricity's share in global energy use from 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably through renewable sources.
